summary: Abram returns from Egypt wealthy, but his and Lot’s growing herds lead their herdsmen into conflict. Abram offers Lot first choice, Lot moves toward Sodom, and Yahweh renews the land and offspring promise to Abram, who settles near Mamre and builds an altar.
whyItMatters: The chapter shows a peaceful response to family conflict while also placing Lot near a city the narrator calls wicked. The renewed promise comes after separation and must be read alongside the existing inhabitants of the land.

context.author: Genesis names no historical writer. Jewish and Christian tradition associates the Torah with Moses; the book briefing describes older traditions shaped into a final literary form, without a settled account of every stage.
context.audience: The book addresses Israel through a story of shared human origins and the family from whom Israel traces its ancestry; no single first audience is named in this chapter.
context.date: The narrated events belong to primeval or ancestral time, not to a securely dated writing event. Major stages of Genesis are often placed across the monarchic to Persian periods, with exact models and dates debated.
context.setting: The South, Bethel and Ai, the Jordan plain toward Sodom, and Mamre near Hebron.
context.literaryForm: Pasture-conflict and separation narrative followed by a renewed land promise and movement notice.

before.text: Pharaoh has expelled Abram with Sarai and all his possessions after the Egyptian crisis. Lot has remained part of the traveling household.

here.text: The conflict is over whether two wealthy households can share pasture; Lot chooses the watered plain, then Abram hears a renewed promise.

after.text: War among regional kings reaches Sodom, and Lot is taken captive, drawing Abram into a rescue expedition.

outline.heading: Return and accumulated wealth
outline.note: Abram returns to the earlier altar near Bethel with livestock and goods.

outline.heading: Pasture conflict and peace offer
outline.note: The two households cannot share the land easily, and Abram offers Lot a choice.

outline.heading: Lot chooses the plain
outline.note: Lot moves toward well-watered land and Sodom, whose people the narrator calls wicked.

outline.heading: Land and offspring promise renewed
outline.note: Yahweh speaks after the separation; Abram travels to Mamre and builds an altar.

keyVerses.text: Abram said to Lot, “Please, let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herdsmen and my herdsmen; for we are relatives.
keyVerses.why: Abram frames separation as a way to avoid strife between relatives.

keyVerses.text: So Lot chose the Plain of the Jordan for himself. Lot traveled east, and they separated themselves from one another.
keyVerses.why: Lot’s chosen direction marks the family split and leads toward Sodom.

keyVerses.text: I will make your offspring as the dust of the earth, so that if a man can count the dust of the earth, then your offspring may also be counted.
keyVerses.why: The dust image expands the offspring promise despite the household separation.

questions.question: Why do Abram and Lot separate?
questions.answer: Both have substantial flocks, herds, and tents, and the land cannot support them together without conflict between herdsmen. Abram proposes separation to preserve peace between relatives.

questions.question: Who are “herdsmen” in the dispute?
questions.answer: They are the workers tending Abram’s and Lot’s livestock. Their quarrel makes the households’ material pressure visible, even though Abram addresses the solution directly to Lot.

questions.question: What attracts Lot to the Jordan plain?
questions.answer: He sees that it is well watered everywhere, compared by the narrator to a garden and to Egypt. He chooses it and moves east, while the narrator also warns that Sodom’s people are wicked.

questions.question: Is Lot blamed here for the later destruction of Sodom?
questions.answer: This chapter says he chooses the plain and moves near Sodom, and it states that the city’s people are wicked. It does not say Lot causes that wickedness or yet narrate Sodom’s destruction.

questions.question: When is the land promise renewed?
questions.answer: Yahweh speaks after Lot separates, asks Abram to look in every direction, and promises land to Abram and his offspring. The timing puts promise beside a reduced household, not alongside a settled possession already achieved.

questions.question: Can “forever” in the land promise be turned into an immediate modern title deed?
questions.answer: The speech makes a broad promise within this ancestral narrative, while the same chapter shows other peoples living in the land and Abram living in tents. It does not supply a modern political map or resolve later competing claims.

questions.question: What is Mamre here?
questions.answer: The oaks of Mamre are the place near Hebron where Abram moves his tent after the promise. He builds an altar there, making it a named stop in his unsettled journey.

questions.question: Why does Abram return to his first altar?
questions.answer: The return from Egypt brings him to the place between Bethel and Ai where he had previously worshiped. Calling on Yahweh’s name there links the post-famine journey with his earlier arrival in Canaan.

glossary.def: Workers responsible for livestock whose dispute triggers the household separation.
The well-watered Jordan region Lot chooses as his place to live.
The oaks near Hebron where Abram later tents and builds an altar.
